data.title: Persona
data.tagline: An evidence-based model of a target user's behavior, goals, and concerns
data.learningOutcome: You can point to the homepage copy or action that addresses a persona's goal and concern.
data.description: When writing homepage copy, a team can synthesize interview or usage notes: freelance designers want potential clients to see their work quickly, and they worry about building and maintaining a site. A persona makes those goals, behavior, and concerns a reference for checking whether the homepage offers a portfolio and an easy way to start. It remains a model to validate; demographic details without evidence are not facts.

learning.assumes: You are unsure who a product or page is written for, or the team describes the target user differently.
learning.outcome: You can point to the homepage copy or action that addresses a persona's goal and concern.

distinctions.label: Market segment
distinctions.explanation: A market segment divides people into groups by data; a persona concentrates one group into a single person for alignment.

distinctions.label: User journey
distinctions.explanation: A user journey describes behavior over time; a persona describes who this is.

explanation.title: Who the copy speaks to
explanation.text: Synthesize goals, behavior, and concerns from interviews or usage notes, then check whether the heading, copy, and action respond. Do not add unsupported details such as age.

explanation.title: What to do first
explanation.text: Goals and context help compare priorities, but a persona supplies evidence for a decision—it does not replace product judgment or user validation.

explanation.title: Acceptance has a basis
explanation.text: Turn 'Can the target user understand this and find the next step?' into a question to check in an interview or page observation.

data.boundary: A persona is a representative model synthesized from evidence, not an invented age, job, and name, and it does not describe every user. When research is missing, label assumptions for validation and check them through interviews or usage observation.

lessonPractice.title: Interviews suggest freelance designers want clients to see their work but worry they cannot build a website. What should the homepage show first?

options.label: Lead with a portfolio and an easy way to get started, then check the copy with interviewees
options.feedback: Correct. A portfolio supports the goal of showing work, and a clear start path addresses the concern about building a site. Validate the copy with target users before release.

options.label: List every product feature and let visitors decide whether it fits
options.feedback: A feature list does not explain how to show work or how someone with no site-building experience can start.

options.label: Add 'for users over 35' to make the audience specific
options.feedback: The notes give no evidence for age. Base the persona on observed goals, behavior, and concerns instead of inventing demographics.

data.agentPrompt: Use these interview notes to revise the homepage: 'Freelance designers want clients to see their work quickly and worry they cannot build a website.' Treat this as a persona hypothesis to validate; do not invent an age or other unsupported detail. Make the headline and first action address the goal and concern, and list what still needs user validation.

references.title: Personas vs. Jobs to Be Done
